nameStory: The ash-tree bolete gets its straightforward name from its close association with ash trees, where it's almost always found growing nearby. Unlike many fungi with mysterious or poetic names, this one tells you exactly where to look for it - making it a favorite among beginning mushroom hunters who appreciate such helpful hints from nature.
description: The ash-tree bolete is a distinctive mushroom with a fan-shaped or semicircular cap that grows directly from the ground near ash trees. Its most notable feature is the unusual honeycomb-like or maze-like pattern of pores on the underside instead of typical round pores. The cap is typically brownish to tan colored and can reach 3-6 inches across, with a short, stubby stem that's often off-center or missing entirely.

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: The underside has a distinctive honeycomb or maze-like pattern of large, angular pores that look almost gill-like, completely different from the small round pores of typical boletes

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Fan-shaped to semicircular, brownish-tan to yellowish-brown, with a slightly fuzzy or velvety texture when young, becoming smoother with age

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Very short and stubby, often off-center or completely absent, pale colored and firm to the touch

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Olive-brown to yellowish-brown when spores are collected on white paper

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Mild, earthy mushroom smell without any strong or unpleasant odors

habitat: Look for ash-tree boletes growing from the ground in deciduous forests where ash trees are present, particularly in rich, moist soils. They're most commonly found in mixed hardwood forests at lower to middle elevations throughout New England. The mushrooms typically appear within 20-30 feet of living ash trees, often in small clusters.

seasonality.spring: No fruiting occurs in spring as soil temperatures are too cool for this species.
seasonality.summer: Peak fruiting season begins in mid to late summer, especially after periods of warm, humid weather and adequate rainfall.
seasonality.fall: Continues fruiting into early fall, with the best specimens often found in September when conditions remain warm and moist.
seasonality.winter: No active fruiting in winter, though dried specimens may persist on the forest floor.

funFact: The ash-tree bolete has one of nature's most unusual three-way partnerships - it depends on a special relationship with both ash tree roots AND aphids that live on those roots, making it one of the few mushrooms that literally can't exist without insects!
confusionNotes: The maze-like pore pattern is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other mushrooms once you see the underside. However, from above, beginners might mistake it for oyster mushrooms or other bracket fungi - always check the pores underneath for the characteristic honeycomb pattern.
contextualKnowledge: With ash trees under severe threat from the emerald ash borer beetle across New England, the ash-tree bolete may become increasingly rare in areas where ash trees have died off, making it an important species to document when found.
compareHints: The ash-tree bolete is the only species in its genus Boletinellus found in New England, making it unique in the region. It differs from other boletes in the Boletinellaceae family by its distinctive maze-like pores rather than round tubes, its fan-shaped growth form, and its obligate association with ash trees. While other boletes may grow near various trees, none share this species' specific three-way relationship with ash trees and aphids.
